Watercolor on paper. 24 13/16 x 29 1/2 in. National Academy of Design, New York, NY. Gift of the artist. ©1970 Yasu Eguchi. NEW YORK, NY .- The National Academy of Design presents Shelter from the Storm: An Artist's Eye with Stan Allen and Polly Apfelbaum, an exhibition on view September 17, 2026 through January 16, 2027, at the National Academy's gallery, 519 West 26th Street, 2nd Floor, New York City. Marking the return of The Artist's Eye exhibition series for the first time since 2013, the exhibition brings together eighty works from the Academy's collection to examine how artists and architects have responded to periods of upheaval, uncertainty, and transformation throughout American history. Co-curated by architect Stan Allen and artist Polly Apfelbaum, Shelter from the Storm serves as the culminating exhibition of the National Academy's bicentennial anniversary year and is the largest collection-based exhibition to be presented in the Academy’s Chelsea space since it opened in September 2023. Launched in 1992, The Artist's Eye invites a National Academician to curate an exhibition around a theme of their choosing, drawn from the Academy's historic collection of more than 8,000 works of art and architecture donated by Academicians upon their election to the Academy. Previous Artist’s Eye curators have included Paul Cadmus, Jane Freilicher, Jacob Lawrence, Philip Pearlstein, and Judith Shea, among others. In addition to being the first time an Artist’s Eye exhibition is co-curated by two Academicians, this will also be the first time an architect is curating. For Shelter from the Storm, Allen and Apfelbaum draw on decades of artistic dialogue and shared inquiry as a married couple to explore how artists and architects have navigated moments of social change, conflict, displacement, loss, and renewal. With work spanning more than two centuries–from 1788 to the present–the exhibition reveals unexpected connections among paintings, sculptures, drawings, architectural works, and mixed-media pieces, one-third of which are being publicly exhibited for the first time. In total, 54 artists and architects are included in the show, 23 of whom are still actively practicing. The exhibition takes inspiration from the National Academy's own history. Since its founding in 1825, the Academy has persevered through war, social upheaval, movements for civil rights and women's suffrage, public health crises, and profound cultural transformation. Opening at another moment of uncertainty and polarization in the United States, Shelter from the Storm considers how artists and architects have witnessed, interpreted, and responded to these experiences, offering a nuanced portrait of resilience across generations. As Allen and Apfelbaum write in their exhibition essay, “The works we have selected for Shelter from the Storm trace the many ways–direct and indirect–that artists have responded to [the United States’] complex two-hundred-year history: a body of work that bears witness to conflict, change and loss; to trauma, isolation, exclusion and despair...But this is not just a litany of loss…we have selected works of stubborn beauty that offer not consolation or easy comfort, but refuge and measured hope; light in dark times. Art cannot alter history, but works of art can extend the horizon of imagination, and help us to envision alternative histories and alternative futures.” The final checklist is the result of more than a year of exploration, research, and discovery by the curators in the Academy’s expansive collection storage. By reinterpreting historic works through the distinct perspectives of an architect and an artist, Allen and Apfelbaum uncover new relationships across media, eras, and lived experiences. Their selections illuminate the ways artists create meaning in times of anxiety and invite audiences to consider the enduring role of art and architecture in shaping collective memory. Featured works include Howardena Pindell's Autobiography: Hiroshima Disguised (1982), a powerful mixed-media installation that reflects on the enduring consequences of nuclear warfare and the political climate of its time, and Annette Lemieux's Boots on the Ground (2022), a work that employs everyday objects to examine the language and realities of military conflict in an era marked by both global unrest and domestic division. These themes are echoed in selections from the Academy's architectural holdings, including photographs and renderings of monuments, memorials, cemeteries, and museums dedicated to preserving the memory of war and its victims. Among them is Mack Scogin Merrill Elam Architects' unbuilt proposal for the Museum of the Second World War, Gdańsk, Poland (2010), which demonstrates architecture's unique capacity to engage with collective remembrance and historical reflection. Balancing these meditations on conflict are works that evoke recovery and hope. Paul Resika's The End of the Hurricane (1979) captures a moment of calm after turmoil, reflecting the artist's lifelong commitment to transforming observed landscapes into deeply personal and spiritual expressions. Together, the works on view invite visitors to consider the ways art and architecture help us confront the past, navigate the present, and imagine a more hopeful future. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crl7.text: Image source, Family/Reuters By Yolande Knell Â and Â Lucy Williamson ,Â Middle East correspondents ,Â Reporting from Jerusalem Published 19 August 2026 The Israeli military has confirmed for the first time that it opened fire on a car carrying five-year-old Palestinian girl Hind Rajab, who was killed along with six relatives in Gaza in 2024. Rajab initially survived the attack and answered a telephone call during which she pleaded for help. The call lasted hours. An ambulance sent to reach her â in a move co-ordinated with the Israeli army - was then shelled, killing two paramedics. Hind's body was recovered days later, along with the others killed. In a statement, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said that it would open a criminal investigation into Hind, her family and the paramedics' killings, as well as the killing of 15 Palestinians, including medics and a UN worker, in March 2025. 'Will you come and get me?' Gaza girl's desperate plea before losing contact Published 5 February 2024 Families' agonising search for answers as thousands still missing in Gaza Published 19 hours ago Film about Gaza child's killing gets record ovation at Venice Published 4 September 2025 Both incidents drew international condemnation. The IDF said of the killing of Hind: "Due to alleged failures in the co-ordination of the movement of the Palestine Red Crescent ambulance, it has been decided to initiate a criminal investigation of the incident by Military Police Criminal Investigation Division." It added that the findings of its examination "indicate that IDF troops fired at a vehicle" that was "travelling contrary to the advanced notice that had been published in an announcement by the IDF Spokesperson to residents of the area". The IDF initially stated that none of its troops were in the area at the time of Hind's killing. However, that suggestion was soon questioned. The IDF later said it had "conducted raids on terror targets" with forces operating in neighbourhoods in Gaza City, including Tel al-Hawa, where Hind was located. Hind's killing was internationally condemned after a desperate recording of her speaking to paramedics of the Palestinian Red Crescent Society (PRCS) was broadcast around the world. The sound of Hind's fragile voice on the other of the line that day haunted the Red Crescent operators long after her death, as she described seeing tanks directly in front of the car, moving towards her. "Hide under the seats," the operators told her. "Don't let anyone see you." Operator Rana Faqih stayed on the line with Hind for hours, as the Red Crescent team appealed to the Israeli army to allow their ambulance to access the location. Faqih said the child appealed to her over and over again for someone to come and rescue her. "At one point, she told me it was getting dark," Rana told the BBC in February 2024. "She was scared. She asked me how far away my house was. I felt paralysed and helpless." Three hours after the call began, an ambulance was finally cleared to approach the area, and was despatched to rescue Hind. It was after dark when the crew - Yusuf al-Zeino and Ahmed al-Madhoun - notified operators that they were nearing the location, and were about to be checked for entry by Israeli forces. It was the last operators heard from them â or from Hind. After that, the line to both paramedics, and to the girl they came to rescue, disconnected for good. The PRCS later confirmed that both Yusuf al-Zeino and Ahmed al-Madhoun were killed when the ambulance was bombed by Israeli forces. "The [Israeli] occupation deliberately targeted the Red Crescent crew despite obtaining prior coordination to allow the ambulance to arrive at the scene to rescue the child Hind," the organisation said in a statement. The story was made into an Oscar-nominated film called The Voice of Hind Rajab. The UN cited her case in a commission of inquiry, accusing Israel of war crimes, which it denies. Following the Israeli army's announcement, the Hind Rajab Foundation, which is based in Brussels and seeks to address alleged Israeli violations in Gaza, said it had "no confidence" in the investigation. "These reported investigations, even if they do occur, should not be mistaken for a genuine step toward justice," it said in a statement. It added that Israel's internal investigations were "fundamentally flawed and cannot be regarded as credible mechanisms of accountability". The IDF's statement on Wednesday said: "For more than a thousand days, the IDF has been conducting intensive combat across numerous fronts, carrying out a wide range of military missions in an exceptionally complex operational reality. "As part of the IDF's obligations under international law and Israeli domestic law, the IDF examines exceptional incidents that occurred during combat." Aside from the criminal investigation into Hind, her family and the paramedics, the IDF also said it would investigate the killing of 15 Palestinians , after an IDF unit fired on ambulances, a fire engine and a marked UN vehicle, in the Tal al-Sultan area of Rafah in southern Gaza during an emergency call-out early on 23 March 2025. Their bodies were found buried in shallow graves a week later next to the crushed vehicles. The Israeli military initially said its troops fired on "suspicious vehicles" driving in darkness with their headlights and emergency lights off. But it later said that account was "mistaken" after a video found on the mobile phone of one of the dead paramedics, Rifaat Radwan, showed the convoy was using its emergency lights. In Wednesday's statement, the IDF said: "Following review of the findings, having found that the firing conducted during the incident raises a reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct, it has been decided to initiate a criminal investigation of the incident." In three other cases, including the killing of seven World Central Kitchen employees in Deir al-Balah two years ago, and four employees of MÃ©decins Sans FrontiÃ¨res (MSF), who were killed in two incidents, the IDF said it had not found grounds for criminal investigations. World Central Kitchen said it "strongly" condemned the Israeli military prosecutor's account of the deaths of its seven colleagues in 2024 and demanded an independent investigation. This is the first time a comprehensive IDF report on alleged war crimes has been published since the start of the Gaza war, triggered by the Hamas-led attacks on Israel on 7 October 2023. More than 73,000 people have been killed in Gaza since Israel launched its military campaign, including about 1,200 since a ceasefire was announced last October, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry - figures considered reliable by the UN . The IDF is under pressure to show it investigates itself to try to stave off international legal action, most notably from the International Criminal Court. It aims to counter accusations that it has committed war crimes and that there is impunity for its forces. However, Israeli rights groups say that criminal investigations of Israeli forces rarely lead to convictions. Ziv Stahl, executive director of Israeli human rights group Yesh Din, told the BBC that "almost no indictments are filed in relation to the number of complaints against soldiers and commanders for offences committed. "In the even more rare cases where soldiers or commanders are convicted, they receive disproportionately lenient sentences that bear little relation to the severity of the offences." Photograph: Anna Barclay/Getty Images View image in fullscreen The launch of the new EV, which can reach 60mph in 4.3 seconds, marks a milestone departure from cars powered by fossil fuels for Jaguar Land Rover. Photograph: Anna Barclay/Getty Images Jaguar Land Rover Range Rover launches its first electric vehicle, with starting price of £154,070 Fully electric SUV unveiled after year-long delay and will be built at Jaguar Land Rover’s plant in Solihull Rob Davies Wed 2 Sep 2026 05.08 EDT Last modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 05.24 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Range Rover has launched its first electric vehicle – a year later than planned – offering a greener option for fans of gargantuan British-made SUVs who are also conscious about the climate crisis. Due to be built in Solihull, the home of the marque since 1970, the vehicle comes with an eye-watering price tag, starting at £154,070. However, the delayed launch marks a milestone departure from cars powered by fossil fuels for Jaguar Land Rover (JLR), which is owned by India’s Tata Motors but headquartered in Coventry in the UK. It also provides a much-needed moment of positivity for JLR, which reported falling profits earlier this year as it counted the cost of Donald Trump’s tariff wars and supply chain disruption after a crippling cyber-attack last year . JLR said it had given extra training to 10,500 staff working on the project and that the car had undergone testing equivalent to 38 trips around the world, more than any other Range Rover. The company said the luxury vehicle, which can reach 60mph in 4.3 seconds, heralded “a new era of enhanced refinement and capability”. While the model’s electric powertrain will limit its impact on the environment compared with JLR’s petrol and diesel models, SUVs of its size are consistently linked to higher numbers of road deaths in accidents involving pedestrians. However, Ranger Rover’s bespoke commissioning service does mean that buyers have an “extended choice of near limitless paint colours and finishes, elevated materials, tailored colour combinations and personalisation details including unique embroidery”. Martin Limpert, the managing director of Range Rover, said the vehicle was the end product of a “decade of considered engineering and technological development”. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning after newsletter promotion Production at Solihull will be supported by the automaker’s propulsion manufacturing centre, in Wolverhampton, which makes battery packs and electric drive units, as well as traditional internal combustion engines. The conventional, “below the nuclear threshold” capabilities would be used to target command posts, airfields, missile launchers, and supply hubs. The ministry’s strategy consists of a four-part plan. The first phase involves deploying a new, low-cost cruise missile starting in 2027. The second phase focuses on the United States, with an internal goal to achieve initial operational readiness of US Typhon launchers armed with Tomahawk missiles by the end of the decade, providing Berlin with a proven interim weapon. Advertisement The final two phases of the plan involve the joint development of highly advanced weapon systems with the United Kingdom, slated for introduction by the middle of the next decade. According to the internal documents, the capacity building will require “nearly €12 billion” in state funds. The funding has not yet been approved but was submitted as part of the state budget planning process. A spokesperson for the German Defense Ministry declined to comment to Politico on the specific figures or individual programs, stating that the ministry will only comment after parliamentary review. Russian hybrid threats in Germany The military buildup comes as Germany weighs taking diplomatic action against Moscow over mounting hybrid security threats. The German government is currently reviewing the international legal basis for the Russian House cultural center in Berlin and has not ruled out terminating a 2011 bilateral agreement that allows it to operate. Germany’s next opportunity to terminate the agreement takes effect in June 2027, requiring Berlin to notify Moscow by Dec. 6, 2026. Advertisement The Foreign Ministry cited “Russia’s increasing hybrid activities” as the primary reason for the review. The Russian House, operated by the sanctioned Russian state agency Rossotrudnichestvo, has traditionally hosted cultural events but is now facing heightened scrutiny. The debate over the cultural center follows a recent incident where an explosive-laden drone was discovered near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo aircraft at the Leipzig/Halle Airport. German federal prosecutors have taken over the investigation into the drone. Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt characterized the incident as a potential “hybrid attack scenario” involving a foreign power, warning that Germany has become a daily target for espionage, sabotage, and cyberattacks. https://www.politico.eu/article/will-chr.text: ÉPREVILLE–EN-LIEUVIN, France – As European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde shook hands and tasted oysters on the bucolic grounds of a Norman manor on Saturday, some might have seen a presidential candidate in waiting. But, Lagarde swears, there is nothing to see here. Speaking as a special guest at the Fête de la Pomme , an apple-themed political gathering organized by Normandy's regional president Hervé Morin, Lagarde dodged questions over her involvement in the French presidential race and her early departure from the ECB — despite mounting speculation on both matters. Advertisement Advertisement On stage, she even encouraged reporters who made the trip to Normandy to cover her potential political comeback to pack up early, promising that they would be disappointed. But there are signs suggesting that the ECB chief, who entered into politics during the presidency of France's apple-loving Jacques Chirac, is increasingly willing to weigh in on the campaign. While she promised to stay at least until the end of the year, Lagarde previously refused to rule out leaving before the end of her term, which ends in October 2027. Earlier this week, she announced that she would publish her first autobiography, Lady First , in January. She also waded into the French presidential debate by rejecting French far-left presidential contender Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s proposal to wipe out government debt. Her presence at the apple festival in the 15th-century Manoir de la Fortière — an unconventional locale for a central banker's speech — might be yet another signal. Opening the event, Morin said that he tried to invite her for years but never managed to make it work. Until this year. “Everyone is happy to have you here and I realized to what extent you have an exceptional reputation,” said Morin, who worked with Lagarde when they both served as ministers under conservative president Nicolas Sarkozy, including during the 2008 financial crisis. Advertisement Advertisement While Lagarde declined to say whether she would become involved in the campaign, participants to Morin’s annual political rally didn’t rule that out. “Several people mention Lagarde as a presidential candidate, but she is the only one who can answer that question,” said centrist senator Catherine Morin-Desailly. “She is a Norman, French and European figure who must, of course, play an active role in helping to shape and develop future platforms for the presidential election. Good candidates will call on her expertise, and I hope they do.” With centrist candidates Gabriel Attal and Edouard Philippe competing against each other and Bruno Retailleau, the leader of the conservative Les Républicains, also taking part in the race, the center-right side of the presidential spectrum is already crowded. For Kristina Pluchet, a senator from Les Républicains who backs Retailleau, other candidates including Christine Lagarde could very well join the race, but they should compete in a primary election. With French bond yields rising and the government led by Sébastien Lecornu struggling to cut the deficit , Lagarde’s financial résumé could prove to be an asset — although she complained to a local producer that the oysters she had during her time as the International Monetary Fund boss in New York were washed with chlorine. Advertisement Advertisement The ECB President didn’t give any hint on her political future in her speech. Instead, she used repeated references to calvados, Normandy's internationally famous apple brandy, to make the case for the benefits of EU membership. She said that calvados, which could be found on the stands of the fête, can be better exported across the world thanks to the EU’s trade policy and is protected by the bloc’s geographical indications. And, unlike calvados which can flow freely between member states without tariffs, capital and services still face internal barriers imposed by member countries, she added. “It is no surprise, then, that many of the people who want to build something new leave Europe altogether,” Lagarde said, calling for the emergence of a real capital markets union to rival the U.S.. As she walked back to a German-plated grey Mercedes S-Class, wearing a scarf with Normandy's two-leopards flag, Lagarde stopped for selfies, but kept sidestepping questions about her future.

https://www.politico.eu/article/ukraine-.text: A large-scale overnight drone attack on Moscow by Ukraine killed at least two people and damaged a major oil refinery, Moscow’s regional governor Andrey Vorobyov said Sunday — the last day of voting in Russia’s parliamentary elections. “Overnight, the Moscow Region was subjected to a massive drone attack,” said Vorobyov , adding that 400 people had been evacuated from an apartment building. Sergei Sobyanin, the city’s mayor, said more than 1,600 drones were intercepted and shot down, with 450 of them headed for the Russian capital. “The biggest attack by enemy drones has been repelled,” he said on Telegram . “This unprecedented attack was clearly planned with the aim of disrupting the ⁠elections. The enemy did not succeed.” Advertisement Advertisement Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed attacks had been carried out against infrastructure facilities in and around Moscow. “Our long-range responses had a very significant impact in the Moscow region last night. One of Russia’s key oil industry facilities and the aggressor’s logistics facility were hit,” he said on X . Russian voters have been heading to the polls this weekend in the first parliamentary elections since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Russian President Vladimir Putin’s ruling United Russia party is expected to retain its dominance in the parliament and present the win as proof of public support for the war in Ukraine. “Your choice, and your will, will once ​again demonstrate that millions of people stand behind our soldiers, that we are a united people bound together by shared values, historical memory, and love for our homeland, and that no one will succeed in dividing or intimidating us,” Putin said in a televised address before the vote. On Saturday, Ukrainian officials said three children and a woman had died in Russian attacks on the Vyshgorod district of Kyiv. Regional Governor Tymur Tkachenko said Sunday a child who was injured in Saturday’s attack had died in hospital.

https://www.dw.com/en/france-hundreds-ar.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NYRd High school students in France are protesting overcrowded classes, heavy workloads, poor-quality learning materials and teacher shortages Image: Raphael Lafargue/ABACA/IMAGO Advertisement Security forces in France on Wednesday detained over 600 people as protests at high schools in parts of the country have intensified. Authorities said violent clashes and arson attacks have also left dozens of security personnel wounded. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez condemned what he called an "escalation of violence" outside certain schools. The violence left 83 police officers and gendarmes wounded on Wednesday, he said, adding that 32 teachers and pupils were also injured. The protests affected 356 schools, the minister noted. He slammed the "targeting of law enforcement officers, the throwing of projectiles, acts of violence, verbal abuse, attempted arson, and what amounts... to urban violence." The student protest movement began in the Ile-de-France region around the capital, Paris, but has since spread to other regions Image: Kenzo Tribouillard/AFP Why are students protesting? Teenagers at French lycées (equivalent to US high schools) have been blockading their schools since last week. They are protesting overcrowded classes, heavy workloads, poor-quality learning materials and teacher shortages. "There are cockroaches and rats everywhere in the school," Fadila, a 17-year-old student, told the Reuters news agency. She said temperatures in classrooms could swing from sweltering to below freezing, depending on the weather. The movement began in the Ile-de-France region around the capital, Paris, but has since spread to other regions. The cities worst affected Wednesday include Paris, Bordeaux in the southwest and Lyon in the southeast, and the northern city of Lille, where police again used tear gas in clashes, the AFP news agency reported. What did the government say? President Emmanuel Macron said the young people's concerns were legitimate but could in no way justify violence and attacks on police officers and teachers, among others. "High schools are meant to be open and to share knowledge. They are not meant to be blockaded or to have trash ⁠cans set on fire," he told reporters in Madrid. Teenagers at French lycees have been blockading their schools since last week Image: Raphael Lafargue/ABACA/IMAGO Both Macron and Nunez accused far-left groups of inciting violence during the protests. "We observed that, in certain places, ⁠there were ​individuals acting as agitators — people who, moreover, moved from one school to another to stir ​up high school and other students and incite them to commit acts of violence," Nunez said. Over the past few days, officials and politicians have denounced the left-wing La France Insoumise (France Unbowed or LFI) party and its presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon for rhetoric they said was stoking students' anger. On Monday, Melenchon had accused the government of implementing a "crackdown" with "obvious racist undertones." "Hands off our youth!" he wrote on social media, while encouraging LFI activists and officials to support the protests wherever they could. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu called the accusation of racism "an insult" and accused Melenchon of "racializing a debate about student security and adding to division where a responsible politician should be looking to restore calm."
